> obligations after notice). 
> Any denial of a §605B request must be lawful, specific, and expressed in a manner 
> compliant with the statute. Unsupported assertions that documentation is “invalid,” without 
> explanation, do not satisfy federal law. 
> 13258290.1.2-5
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 9>
> 
> III. FAILURE TO RESPOND TO CERTIFIED-MAIL NOTICE 
> TransUnion failed to respond to multiple certified-mail notices, including executive-level 
> correspondence, despite proof of delivery. 
> Once a consumer reporting agency receives actual notice of statutory violations: 
> ● Continued inaction constitutes reckless disregard; 
> ● Silence after notice constitutes ratification of unlawful practices; and 
> ● Liability escalates from negligence to willful non-compliance under 15 U.S.C. §1681n. 
> TransUnion was given ample opportunity to cure. It chose not to. 
> Courts routinely distinguish administrative error from willful non-compliance based on how an 
> agency responds after receiving clear, repeated notice of statutory violations. 
> At this stage, the continued denial of relief is no longer attributable to an initial processing error 
> or factual uncertainty. The record reflects repeated notice, repeated clarification of statutory 
> obligations, and continued reliance on non-statutory rationales. Under these circumstances, 
> courts evaluate the conduct of the consumer reporting agency based on its post-notice 
> decision-making, not the original dispute. 
> IV. FACTUAL TIMELINE OF NON-COMPLIANCE 
> (DOCUMENTED) 
> The following timeline is supported by certified-mail receipts, CFPB complaint records, and 
> recorded communications: 
> June 2025 
> ● I submitted a complete FCRA §605B identity theft package, including a valid FTC 
> Identity Theft Report, proof of identity and address, written identification of alleged 
> fraudulent hard inquiries, and a sworn statement of non-authorization. 
> ● Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion’s statutory deadline to block the identified 
> information expired four (4) business days after receipt. 
> June - July 2025 
> ● TransUnion failed to block the alleged fraudulent inquiries within the statutory timeframe. 
> ● Multiple certified-mail follow-up notices were sent and delivered. 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 9>
> 
> ● TransUnion repeatedly asserted the documentation was “invalid,” without identifying 
> any deficiency or statutory basis, and without issuing a legally compliant denial under 
> §605B(c). 
> July - August 2025 
> ● TransUnion: 
> ○ Refused to act pending creditor responses, 
> ○ Cited internal “company policy” and “system limitations,” 
> ○ Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file. 
> Executive-Level Notice 
> ● A final executive-level demand was sent via certified mail with documented signature 
> proof of delivery & received to TransUnion leadership. 
> ● No response was provided, despite confirmed delivery. 
> As of the date of this notice, TransUnion remains more than 60 days beyond the statutory 
> deadline with no lawful denial and no corrective action. 
> V. ACTUAL DAMAGES INCURRED (CAUSATION 
> ESTABLISHED) 
> Despite actual notice and multiple compliant submissions, TransUnion continued to maintain 
> and report the identified inquiries, compounding harm and escalating liability. 
> Courts evaluating FCRA claims have recognized that actual damages are not limited to 
> formal credit denials, and may include documented emotional distress, administrative 
> burden, and prolonged interference with financial activities where supported by 
> competent evidence. 
> As a direct and foreseeable result of TransUnion’s conduct, I have incurred: 
> A. Credit & Financial Harm 
> ● Interference with credit approvals due to continued reporting of alleged fraudulent 
> inquiries; 
> ● Forced delays and denials attributable to TransUnion’s failure to comply with §605B. 
> B. Out-of-Pocket Expenses 
> 13258290.1.3-5
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 9>
> 
> ● Certified mail fees (multiple submissions and recipients); 
> ● Notary services; 
> ● Printing, copying, and document preparation costs. 
> C. Time Loss & Administrative Burden 
> ● Dozens of hours spent researching federal statutes and regulatory guidance, preparing 
> legally compliant affidavits and submissions, drafting formal correspondence, filing and 
> responding to multiple CFPB complaints, and engaging in recorded calls with 
> TransUnion personnel repeating unlawful denial rationales. 
> Courts have repeatedly held that actual damages under the FCRA include time spent correcting 
> inaccuracies, administrative burden, and interference with financial opportunities, even in the 
> absence of a formal credit denial. See Guimond v. Trans Union Credit Info. Co., 45 F.3d 1329 
> (9th Cir. 1995); Philbin v. Trans Union Corp., 101 F.3d 957 (3d Cir. 1996). 
> This time constitutes compensable actual damages, including the reasonable value of work 
> ordinarily billed by legal counsel. 
> VI. STATUTORY DAMAGES & PENALTIES (ACCRUED) 
> Based on documented conduct: 
> ● Statutory damages (15 U.S.C. §1681n): 
> 52 violations × $1,000 = $52,000 
> ● Actual damages (§1681n / §1681o): 
> Credit harm, time loss, administrative costs, and legal research: $25,000–$40,000+ 
> ● Punitive damages (§1681n): 
> Authorized due to post-notice, policy-driven misconduct and reckless disregard of federal 
> law: $150,000+ 
> ○ Where non-compliance persists after repeated notice and the consumer is 
> subjected to prolonged obstruction, courts have found such conduct sufficient to 
> support punitive damages based on the nature, duration, and internal handling of 
> the violations. 
> Where a consumer reporting agency maintains unlawful practices after 
> notice and applies those practices systematically, courts have found 
> punitive damages appropriate to deter future misconduct. See Cortez v. 
> Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010). 
> ● Attorneys’ fees & costs (§1681n(a)(3)): 
> Recoverable by statute and continuing to accrue. 
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 9>
> 
> Total current exposure: $225,000–$260,000+, exclusive of ongoing accrual. 
> VII. STATUTORY VIOLATIONS 
> TransUnion’s conduct constitutes violations of, at minimum: 
> ● §1681c-2(a) - Failure to timely block alleged identity-theft information 
> ● §1681c-2(c) - Imposition of unauthorized conditions 
> ● §1681i(a)(6)(B)(iii) - Failure to issue a lawful denial 
> ● §1681g - Denial of consumer file access 
> ● §1681e(b) - Continued reporting of disputed, allegedly fraudulent information 
> ● §1681n - Willful non-compliance after actual notice 
> ● §1681e(b) - Failure to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible 
> accuracy, including continued reporting and maintenance of information identified as 
> identity-theft related after receipt of a valid FTC Identity Theft Report. 
> Reliance on internal policy or creditor delay to override federal law is per se evidence of 
> willfulness. 
> VIII. DEMAND FOR IMMEDIATE CURE

> Subject: Final Demand for Resolution - FCRA §605B 
> Violations, Damages, and Settlement Request 
> Dear Mr. Cartwright, 
> This is my final, good-faith demand for complete resolution and confidential settlement 
> regarding TransUnion’s repeated, willful violations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act 
> (FCRA), specifically §605B, §611(a)(6), §1681n, and §1681o, as well as violations of active 
> FTC and CFPB Consent Orders (2023). 
> Legal Standard (FCRA §605B and Related Provisions) 
> Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a) (FCRA §605B), CRAs must block fraudulent information within 
> four (4) business days upon receiving: 
> 12195064.1.2-10
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 10>
> 
> ● An FTC identity theft report 
> ● Proof of identity 
> ● Proof of address 
> ● A signed statement identifying the fraudulent data 
> Failure to act requires a written notice of denial with reasons under 15 U.S.C. 
> §1681i(a)(6)(B)(iii) (FCRA §611). 
> Willful violations trigger statutory and punitive damages under §1681n. Negligent violations are 
> actionable under §1681o. 
> Timeline of §605B Submissions (Fully Documented) 
> Since June 5, 2025, I submitted multiple complete §605B identity theft block requests, each 
> via trackable certified mail with full documentation + signature of receipt, including: 
> ● FTC Report 
> ● Notarized Affidavit 
> ● Government ID 
> ● Proof of Address 
> Submission Dates: 
> ● June 9, 2025 (CFPB Complaint 250609-21400333)
> ● June 13, 2025 
> ● June 16, 2025 (CFPB Complaint #250616-21593904) 
> ● July 4th, 2025 (post CFPB Complaint #250704-22063859) 
> Despite meeting every statutory requirement, TransUnion refused to block fraudulent data 
> within 4 business days as required by §605B(a). 
> Denial Reasons Provided by TransUnion 
> (Calls have been recorded, documented, and transcribed via Minnesota 1 way consent laws. 
> Although as a courtesy, all supervisors were informed beforehand of the recording & 
> documentation of the calls) 
> In calls and responses, TransUnion representatives provided unlawful reasons for refusing my 
> §605B requests: 
> 1. Creditor deletion letters required: 
> 12195064.1.3-10
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 10>
> 
> ○ Repeatedly demanded letters from creditors as the “only” way, even though 
> FCRA §605B has no such requirement. 
> 2. “System will not allow” removals: 
> ○ Special Handling Supervisor(s), alleged the system prevented deletion even with 
> valid documentation. 
> 3. Internal policy overrides law: 
> ○ Employees cited “internal policy” to ignore §605B’s 4-day block requirement. 
> 4. Rejecting valid FTC Reports and affidavits: 
> ○ No deficiencies in my documentation were ever identified.
> ○ Rejecting Valid FTC Reports and Affidavits Without Lawful Justification 
> Despite my submission of a valid FTC Identity Theft Report, sworn 
> affidavit, and all required supporting documents under FCRA §605B, 
> TransUnion has repeatedly rejected my request to block fraudulent 
> inquiries without identifying any specific deficiency in the materials 
> provided - either in writing or during recorded phone calls with supervisors 
> from their Fraud Department. 
> This violates multiple provisions of federal law: 
> 1. FCRA §605B(b)(2): 
> "An identity theft report may be a report to a law enforcement 
> agency or the Federal Trade Commission." 
> This statute explicitly confirms that a FTC Identity Theft Report 
> (Affidavit) is legally valid for identity theft blocking requests. It does not 
> require a police report, nor may the CRA reject an FTC report based 
> solely on form preference. 
> 2. FCRA §605B(c)(2): 
> "The consumer reporting agency may not refuse to block the 
> information on the grounds that the consumer has not provided any 
> additional documentation or information, other than as described in 
> subsection (b)." 
> Once the FTC Report, affidavit, ID, and proof of address are submitted 
> - which I provided in full - TransUnion is legally prohibited from requiring 
> any additional documents or imposing further barriers. 
> 12195064.1.4-10
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 10>
> 
> 3. FCRA §611(a)(6)(B)(iii): Requirement to Identify 
> Basis for Denial 
> If a CRA rejects or modifies a request, they are required to 
> provide a specific explanation for the decision. 
> "If the agency determines that the dispute is frivolous 
> or irrelevant, it shall notify the consumer of the 
> determination not later than 5 business days... and 
> shall include the reasons for the determination, and 
> identify any information required to investigate the

> denying my requests. Instead, they issued vague blanket 
> rejections and refused to cite any statutory basis, which 
> violates both 605B and the notice requirements of 611(a). 
> 4. Repeated Non-Disclosure and Obstruction 
> (Documented Behavior): 
> ● Phone Calls: On multiple calls (including with supervisors 
> “Derek” and “Frank” in the Fraud and Special Handling 
> departments), I explicitly asked: 
> “What specific requirement is missing or incorrect in my 
> FTC affidavit or documentation?” 
> They refused to answer and declined to read or cite the 
> specific reason, stating only: 
> “It was rejected by another department.” or “We need
> creditor letters.” 
> ● Written Notices: TransUnion’s written responses also 
> failed to specify any deficiency, instead returning vague 
> statements such as “the documentation is not acceptable” - 
> without identifying what was missing, or how it deviated

> This constitutes a willful evasion of legal duties, as federal law 
> mandates transparency and specificity in denial notices. 
> 12195064.1.5-10
> 
> <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 10>
> 
> 5. Blocking my online account: 
> ○ My account was locked, obstructing my ability to dispute or manage freezes. 
> ○ The reps claimed that this lock is permanent, and there is “nothing” that can be 
> done to unlock it. 
> ○ They also claimed that 605B blocks were not able to be done due to my account 
> be locked due to identity theft; however 605B disputes are exactly for identity 
> theft. Identity theft is not a legally complaint reason to deny such request. 
> 6. No required denial letters: 
> ○ TU failed to issue written denial notices with specific reasons as required by 
> §611(a)(6)(B)(iii). 
> ○ Upon repeated requests Transunion also failed to provide any reasoning or

These submissions were transmitted via certified mail and through the CFPB.
> [L15] Each submission independently triggered TransUnion’s mandatory, non-discretionary obligations under FCRA §605B.

> [L20]

> [L22] 
> [L23] * Failed to provide any lawful written denial explanation or identify curable deficiencies as required by §1681i
> [L24] 
> [L25] * Admitted during recorded calls that no investigation had been conducted
> [L26] 
> [L27] * Restricted access to my consumer file and used that restriction to deny statutory rights
> [L28] 
> [L29] * Failed to respond to executive-level certified notice
> [L30] 
> [L31] This conduct was repeated, occurred after notice, and appears to stem from internal policy rather than lawful compliance.
> [L32] ________________
> [L33] 
> [L34] 
> [L35] Standing and Concrete Harm
> [L36] This matter involves more than a technical or procedural violation.
> [L37] After receiving proper identity-theft documentation, TransUnion continued to publish inaccurate hard inquiries to third-party lenders. As recognized by the Supreme Court in TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, dissemination of inaccurate credit information to third parties constitutes concrete injury.
> [L38] The continued reporting of these inquiries caused reputational and financial harm and fully satisfies Article III standing requirements.

> [L40] 
> [L41]

> [L11] Re: Final Notice of Willful Non-Compliance, Demand for Cure, and Intent to File Suit - FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)
> [L12] To Whom It May Concern,
> [L13] This letter constitutes formal notice of willful and continuing non-compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”) following TransUnion’s repeated failure to comply with mandatory statutory duties, failure to respond to certified-mail notices with proof of delivery, and reliance on unlawful internal practices after actual notice.
> [L14] This notice is sent in good faith to provide one final opportunity to cure.
> [L15] ________________
> [L16] 
> [L17] 
> [L18] I. UNDISPUTED FACTS
> [L19] 1. TransUnion received multiple complete FCRA §605B identity theft submissions, each containing:
> [L20]    * A valid FTC Identity Theft Report
> [L21]    * Proof of identity
> [L22]    * Proof of address
> [L23]    * Written identification of alleged fraudulent hard inquiries
> [L24]    * A sworn statement that the transactions were not authorized
> [L25] 2. Receipt of these submissions is documented by certified-mail return receipts and CFPB complaint records.
> [L26] 3. Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion was required to:
> [L27]    * Block the identified information within four (4) business days, or
> [L28]    * Promptly issue a written denial citing §605B(c) and explaining with specificity the statutory basis for refusal.
> [L29] 4. TransUnion did neither.
> [L30] Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 907 (7th Cir. 2007).
> [L31] ________________
> [L32] 
> [L33] 
> [L34] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES
> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

> [L30] Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 907 (7th Cir. 2007).
> [L31] ________________
> [L32] 
> [L33] 
> [L34] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES
> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

## **EXECUTIVE ORIENTATION (PLAIN-ENGLISH SUMMARY)**

This notice concerns identity-theft–related **hard inquiries** on my TransUnion credit file that **must be blocked by law** once a consumer submits the documents Congress specified in **FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)**.  
I submitted **every required item**; TransUnion **admitted receipt**; yet TransUnion **did not block** the information within **four (4) business days**, repeatedly substituted **non-statutory “policies”** (e.g., creditor deletion letters; freeze requirements), and continued refusals **after notice**, including by **supervisors**, on **recorded calls**.

This letter offers a **final opportunity to cure** without litigation. The statute is **mandatory** and **black-and-white**. Continued non-compliance after notice exposes TransUnion to **willful and reckless violations**, **statutory and punitive damages**, **fees and costs**, and **class-wide exposure**.

---

## **I. STATUTORY FOUNDATION (NON-NEGOTIABLE)**

**FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)** requires a consumer reporting agency (“CRA”) to **block the reporting** of any information identified by the consumer as resulting from alleged identity theft **no later than four (4) business days** after receipt of:

1) Appropriate proof of identity of the consumer;  
2) A copy of an identity-theft report (an **FTC Identity Theft Report qualifies**); and  
3) Identification of the information and a statement that it is **not information relating to any transaction by the consumer**.

**Sole statutory exception (§605B(c))**: A CRA may decline or rescind a block **only if** it determines the block was in error or facts were misrepresented, and must **promptly notify the consumer in writing** with the reasons.  
The statute **does not authorize** creditor deletion letters, credit freezes, fraud alerts, or other extra-statutory prerequisites.

---

## **II. COMPLETENESS & ADMISSIONS**

TransUnion representatives **confirmed receipt** of all §605B items, including:
- Proof of identity;  
- An **FTC Identity Theft Report** executed under penalty of perjury;  
- Identification of the identity-theft–related hard inquiries and a statement of non-authorization.

Despite receipt, TransUnion **did not block** the information within four business days and **never issued** a §605B(c) written determination.

---

## **V. EXTRA-STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS (UNAUTHORIZED)**

TransUnion demanded, inter alia:
- **Creditor deletion letters**;  
- **Credit freeze/fraud alert** as a precondition;  
- Reliance on “belief” without issuing a **§605B(c) written notice**.

## **VI. DEFENSE PREEMPTION (COMPLETE SHUTDOWN)**

**Claimed defense:** TransUnion “believes” I called to unfreeze my file; therefore the inquiries were mine.  
**Fatal defects:**

> [L23] FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2) 
> [L24] To Whom It May Concern, 
> [L25] This letter constitutes formal notice of willful and continuing non-compliance with the Fair 
> [L26] Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”) following TransUnion’s repeated failure to comply with 
> [L27] mandatory statutory duties, failure to respond to certified-mail notices with proof of 
> [L28] delivery, and reliance on unlawful internal practices after actual notice. 
> [L29] This notice is sent in good faith to provide one final opportunity to cure. 
> [L30] I. UNDISPUTED FACTS 
> [L31] 1. TransUnion received multiple complete FCRA §605B identity theft submissions, 
> [L32] each containing: 
> [L33] ○ A valid FTC Identity Theft Report 
> [L34] ○ Proof of identity 
> [L35] ○ Proof of address 
> [L36] ○ Written identification of alleged fraudulent hard inquiries 
> [L37] ○ A sworn statement that the transactions were not authorized 
> [L38] 2. Receipt of these submissions is documented by certified-mail return receipts and 
> [L39] CFPB complaint records. 
> [L40] 3. Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion was required to: 
> [L41] ○ Block the identified information within four (4) business days, or 
> [L42] ○ Promptly issue a written denial citing §605B(c) and explaining with specificity
> [L43] the statutory basis for refusal. 
> [L44] 4. TransUnion did neither.  <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 9> Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, 
> [L45] non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure 
> [L46] to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, 
> [L47] including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 
> [L48] 907 (7th Cir. 2007). 
> [L49] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES 
> [L50] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion: 
> [L51] ● Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were 
> [L52] “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis; 
> [L53] ● Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a); 
> [L54] ● Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g; 
> [L55] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own 
> [L56] credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful 
> [L57] noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010). 
> [L58] ● Conditioned §605B compliance on: 
> [L59] ○ Waiting for creditor responses, 
> [L60] ○ Obtaining creditor confirmation letters, 
> [L61] ○ Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.” 
> [L62] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA. 
> [L63] They are legally void.

> [L1] They are legally void. 
> [L2] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully 
> [L3] under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the 
> [L4] plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of 
> [L5] Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an 
> [L6] unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should 
> [L7] be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) 
> [L8] (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory 
> [L9] obligations after notice). 
> [L10] Any denial of a §605B request must be lawful, specific, and expressed in a manner 
> [L11] compliant with the statute. Unsupported assertions that documentation is “invalid,” without 
> [L12] explanation, do not satisfy federal law. 
> [L13] 13258290.1.2-5 <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 9> III. FAILURE TO RESPOND TO CERTIFIED-MAIL NOTICE 
> [L14] TransUnion failed to respond to multiple certified-mail notices, including executive-level 
> [L15] correspondence, despite proof of delivery. 
> [L16] Once a consumer reporting agency receives actual notice of statutory violations: 
> [L17] ● Continued inaction constitutes reckless disregard; 
> [L18] ● Silence after notice constitutes ratification of unlawful practices; and 
> [L19] ● Liability escalates from negligence to willful non-compliance under 15 U.S.C. §1681n. 
> [L20] TransUnion was given ample opportunity to cure. It chose not to. 
> [L21] Courts routinely distinguish administrative error from willful non-compliance based on how an 
> [L22] agency responds after receiving clear, repeated notice of statutory violations. 
> [L23] At this stage, the continued denial of relief is no longer attributable to an initial processing error 
> [L24] or factual uncertainty. The record reflects repeated notice, repeated clarification of statutory 
> [L25] obligations, and continued reliance on non-statutory rationales. Under these circumstances, 
> [L26] courts evaluate the conduct of the consumer reporting agency based on its post-notice 
> [L27] decision-making, not the original dispute. 
> [L28] IV. FACTUAL TIMELINE OF NON-COMPLIANCE 
> [L29] (DOCUMENTED) 
> [L30] The following timeline is supported by certified-mail receipts, CFPB complaint records, and 
> [L31] recorded communications:

> [L34] Identity Theft Report, proof of identity and address, written identification of alleged 
> [L35] fraudulent hard inquiries, and a sworn statement of non-authorization. 
> [L36] ● Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion’s statutory deadline to block the identified 
> [L37] information expired four (4) business days after receipt. 
> [L38] June - July 2025 
> [L39] ● TransUnion failed to block the alleged fraudulent inquiries within the statutory timeframe. 
> [L40] ● Multiple certified-mail follow-up notices were sent and delivered.  <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 9> ● TransUnion repeatedly asserted the documentation was “invalid,” without identifying 
> [L41] any deficiency or statutory basis, and without issuing a legally compliant denial under 
> [L42] §605B(c). 
> [L43] July - August 2025 
> [L44] ● TransUnion: 
> [L45] ○ Refused to act pending creditor responses, 
> [L46] ○ Cited internal “company policy” and “system limitations,” 
> [L47] ○ Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file. 
> [L48] Executive-Level Notice 
> [L49] ● A final executive-level demand was sent via certified mail with documented signature 
> [L50] proof of delivery & received to TransUnion leadership. 
> [L51] ● No response was provided, despite confirmed delivery.

> [L15] V. ACTUAL DAMAGES INCURRED (CAUSATION ESTABLISHED)
> [L16] 
> [L17] 
> [L18] Despite actual notice and multiple compliant submissions, TransUnion continued to maintain and report the identified inquiries, compounding harm and escalating liability.
> [L19] 
> [L20] 
> [L21] Courts evaluating FCRA claims have recognized that actual damages are not limited to formal credit denials, and may include documented emotional distress, administrative burden, and prolonged interference with financial activities where supported by competent evidence.
> [L22] 
> [L23] 
> [L24] As a direct and foreseeable result of TransUnion’s conduct, I have incurred:
> [L25] A. Credit & Financial Harm
> [L26] * Interference with credit approvals due to continued reporting of alleged fraudulent inquiries;
> [L27] * Forced delays and denials attributable to TransUnion’s failure to comply with §605B.
> [L28] B. Out-of-Pocket Expenses
> [L29] * Certified mail fees (multiple submissions and recipients);
> [L30] * Notary services;
> [L31] * Printing, copying, and document preparation costs.
> [L32] C. Time Loss & Administrative Burden
> [L33] * Dozens of hours spent researching federal statutes and regulatory guidance, preparing legally compliant affidavits and submissions, drafting formal correspondence, filing and responding to multiple CFPB complaints, and engaging in recorded calls with TransUnion personnel repeating unlawful denial rationales.
> [L34] Courts have repeatedly held that actual damages under the FCRA include time spent correcting inaccuracies, administrative burden, and interference with financial opportunities, even in the absence of a formal credit denial. See Guimond v. Trans Union Credit Info. Co., 45 F.3d 1329 (9th Cir. 1995); Philbin v. Trans Union Corp., 101 F.3d 957 (3d Cir. 1996).
> [L35] This time constitutes compensable actual damages, including the reasonable value of work ordinarily billed by legal counsel.
> [L36] ________________
> [L37] 
> [L38] 
> [L39] VI. STATUTORY DAMAGES & PENALTIES (ACCRUED)
> [L40] Based on documented conduct:
> [L41] * Statutory damages (15 U.S.C. §1681n):
> [L42] 52+ documented violations × $1,000 = $52,000+
> [L43] (call recordings + transcripts + certified mail + letters) 
> [L44] * Actual damages (§1681n / §1681o):
> [L45] Credit harm, time loss, administrative costs, and legal research: $25,000-$40,000+
> [L46] * Punitive damages (§1681n):
> [L47] Authorized due to post-notice, policy-driven misconduct and reckless disregard of federal law: $150,000+
> [L48]    * Where non-compliance persists after repeated notice and the consumer is subjected to prolonged obstruction, courts have found such conduct sufficient to support punitive damages based on the nature, duration, and internal handling of the violations.
> [L49] Where a consumer reporting agency maintains unlawful practices after notice and applies those practices systematically, courts have found punitive damages appropriate to deter future misconduct. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L50]    * Attorneys’ fees & costs (§1681n(a)(3)):
> [L51] Recoverable by statute and continuing to accrue.
> [L52] Total current exposure: $225,000–$260,000+, exclusive of ongoing accrual.

> Content source: Source.file

> Citation Marker: fileciteturn7file10
> Mclick Target: "7:10"
> Content Snippet:
> [L1] ﻿Alan Nguyen
> [L2] 11150 Rhode Island Ave S
> [L3] Bloomington, MN 55438
> [L4] SSN: XXX-XX-5713
> [L5] DOB: 07/25/1995
> [L6] TransUnion LLC
> [L7] LEGAL & Office of the General Counsel
> [L8] 555 West Adams Street
> [L9] Chicago, IL 60661
> [L10] Date: January 23rd 2026
> [L11] Re: Final Notice of Willful Non-Compliance, Demand for Cure, and Intent to File Suit - FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)
> [L12] To Whom It May Concern,
> [L13] This letter constitutes formal notice of willful and continuing non-compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”) following TransUnion’s repeated failure to comply with mandatory statutory duties, failure to respond to certified-mail notices with proof of delivery, and reliance on unlawful internal practices after actual notice.
> [L14] This notice is sent in good faith to provide one final opportunity to cure.
> [L15] ________________
> [L16] 
> [L17] 
> [L18] I. UNDISPUTED FACTS
> [L19] 1. TransUnion received multiple complete FCRA §605B identity theft submissions, each containing:
> [L20]    * A valid FTC Identity Theft Report
> [L21]    * Proof of identity
> [L22]    * Proof of address
> [L23]    * Written identification of alleged fraudulent hard inquiries
> [L24]    * A sworn statement that the transactions were not authorized
> [L25] 2. Receipt of these submissions is documented by certified-mail return receipts and CFPB complaint records.
> [L26] 3. Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion was required to:
> [L27]    * Block the identified information within four (4) business days, or
> [L28]    * Promptly issue a written denial citing §605B(c) and explaining with specificity the statutory basis for refusal.
> [L29] 4. TransUnion did neither.
> [L30] Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 907 (7th Cir. 2007).
> [L31] ________________
> [L32] 
> [L33] 
> [L34] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES
> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

> # 【12†Intent litigation TU.txt†file_00000000712871f599e34903cb1ec247】
> Content source: Source.file
> Title: Intent litigation TU.txt
> Citation Marker: fileciteturn7file12
> Mclick Target: "7:12"
> Content Snippet:
> [L1] ﻿Via Certified Mail and CFPB
> [L2] TransUnion LLC - Legal & Compliance Department
> [L3] Re: Alan Nguyen - Notice of Intent to File Suit for FCRA Violations
> [L4] January 8th, 2026
> [L5] 
> [L6] 
> [L7] This letter serves as formal notice of my intent to initiate legal action against TransUnion LLC for willful and reckless violations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”), including but not limited to 15 U.S.C. §§1681c-2, 1681i, 1681e, and 1681g.
> [L8] This notice is provided to allow TransUnion a final opportunity to resolve this matter without litigation.
> [L9] ________________
> [L10] 
> [L11] 
> [L12] Background and Summary
> [L13] I am a verified victim of identity theft.
> [L14] Between June and August 2025, I submitted multiple complete and legally sufficient identity-theft packets to TransUnion, including FTC Identity Theft Reports, notarized affidavits, government identification, proof of address, and written identification of fraudulent hard inquiries. These submissions were transmitted via certified mail and through the CFPB.
> [L15] Each submission independently triggered TransUnion’s mandatory, non-discretionary obligations under FCRA §605B.
> [L16] Despite full compliance on my part, TransUnion failed to meet its statutory duties. Specifically, TransUnion:
> [L17] * Failed to block or delete fraudulent hard inquiries within four business days as required by 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a)
> [L18] 
> [L19] * Continued reporting the inquiries to third-party lenders after receiving identity-theft notice
> [L20] 
> [L21] * Demanded documentation expressly prohibited by statute, including creditor letters and police reports
> [L22] 
> [L23] * Failed to provide any lawful written denial explanation or identify curable deficiencies as required by §1681i
> [L24] 
> [L25] * Admitted during recorded calls that no investigation had been conducted
> [L26] 
> [L27] * Restricted access to my consumer file and used that restriction to deny statutory rights
> [L28] 
> [L29] * Failed to respond to executive-level certified notice
> [L30] 
> [L31] This conduct was repeated, occurred after notice, and appears to stem from internal policy rather than lawful compliance.
> [L32] ________________
> [L33] 
> [L34] 
> [L35] Standing and Concrete Harm
> [L36] This matter involves more than a technical or procedural violation.
> [L37] After receiving proper identity-theft documentation, TransUnion continued to publish inaccurate hard inquiries to third-party lenders. As recognized by the Supreme Court in TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, dissemination of inaccurate credit information to third parties constitutes concrete injury.
> [L38] The continued reporting of these inquiries caused reputational and financial harm and fully satisfies Article III standing requirements.
> [L39] ________________
> [L40] 
> [L41] 
> [L42] Liability and Damages Exposure
> [L43] Based on documented events and conservative, event-based statutory counting:
> [L44]    * Statutory damages: $52,000
> [L45] 
> [L46]    * Actual damages: estimated $25,000–$40,000
> [L47] 
> [L48]    * Punitive damages: authorized under 15 U.S.C. §1681n(a)(2)
> [L49] 
> [L50] Given the repeated, post-notice, and policy-driven nature of the violations, a conservative punitive multiplier of three times statutory damages applies, resulting in $156,000 in punitive exposure.
> [L51] Total damages exposure therefore ranges from $233,000 to $248,000, exclusive of attorneys’ fees and costs, which are independently recoverable.
> [L52] ________________
> [L53] 
> [L54] 
> [L55] Opportunity to Resolve Without Litigation
> [L56] To resolve this matter without filing suit, TransUnion must, within ten (10) business days of receipt of this letter:
> [L57]       1. Permanently delete all fraudulent hard inquiries pursuant to 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2
> [L58] 
> [L59]       2. Restore full access to my TransUnion consumer file pursuant to 15 U.S.C. §1681g
> [L60] 
> [L61]       3. Provide written confirmation of:
> [L62] 
> [L63]          * Inquiry deletions
> [L64] 
> [L65]          * Account access restoration
> [L66] 
> [L67]          * Corrective compliance measures
> [L68] 
> [L69]             4. Offer a confidential settlement in the range of $75,000–$100,000
> [L70] 
> [L71] Any resolution would be without admission of liability and solely to avoid litigation.

BLACK-AND-WHITE RULE

Proof of identity

Identity Theft Report (FTC or police)

Identification of the disputed information

Consumer statement

NO EXCEPTIONS

No discretion

No “internal policy”

No system limitation

No creditor letter requirement

No investigation delay

Information remained reported

2. 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(e) — WILLFUL REFUSAL / IMPROPER RESCISSION
BLACK-AND-WHITE RULE

A CRA may decline or rescind a block ONLY IF it makes a reasonable determination that:

The consumer did not submit an identity theft report, OR

The report was materially false, OR

The consumer obtained goods, services, or money from the transaction

LEGAL REQUIREMENTS

Determination must be fact-based

Must be documented

Must be communicated

TransUnion did not claim fraud in your report

Notice promptly

NOT ALLOWED

This notice concerns identity-theft–related hard inquiries on my TransUnion credit file that must be blocked by law once a consumer submits the documents Congress specified in FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2).

I submitted every required item; TransUnion admitted receipt; yet TransUnion did not block the information within four (4) business days, repeatedly substituted non-statutory “policies” (e.g., creditor deletion letters; freeze requirements), and continued refusals after notice, including by supervisors, on recorded calls.

I. STATUTORY FOUNDATION (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2) requires a consumer reporting agency (“CRA”) to block the reporting of any information identified by the consumer as resulting from alleged identity theft no later than four (4) business days after receipt of:
Appropriate proof of identity of the consumer;
A copy of an identity-theft report (an FTC Identity Theft Report qualifies); and
Identification of the information and a statement that it is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer.


Sole statutory exception (§605B(c)): A CRA may decline or rescind a block only if it determines the block was in error or facts were misrepresented, and must promptly notify the consumer in writing with the reasons.

The statute does not authorize creditor deletion letters, credit freezes, fraud alerts, or other extra-statutory prerequisites.

II. COMPLETENESS & ADMISSIONS
TransUnion representatives confirmed receipt of all §605B items, including:

FCRA § 605B (15 U.S.C. § 1681c-2)
(a) Block. Except as otherwise provided in this section, a consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information
in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from an alleged identity theft, not later than 4
business days after the date of receipt by such agency of—
(1) appropriate proof of the identity of the consumer;
(2) a copy of an identity theft report;
(3) the identification of such information by the consumer; and
(4) a statement by the consumer that the information is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer.
(b) Notification. A consumer reporting agency shall promptly notify the furnisher of information identified by the consumer under
subsection (a) of this section—
(1) that the information may be a result of identity theft;
(2) that an identity theft report has been filed;
(3) that a block has been requested under this section; and
(4) of the effective dates of the block.
(c) Authority to decline or rescind.
(1) In general. A consumer reporting agency may decline to block, or may rescind any block, of information relating to a
consumer under this section, if the consumer reporting agency reasonably determines that—
(A) the information was blocked in error or a block was requested by the consumer in error;
(B) the information was blocked, or a block was requested by the consumer, on the basis of a material misrepresentation
of fact by the consumer relevant to the request to block; or
(C) the consumer obtained possession of goods, services, or money as a result of the blocked transaction or transactions.
(2) Notification to consumer. If a block of information is declined or rescinded under this subsection, the affected consumer
shall be notified promptly, in the same manner as consumers are notified of the reinsertion of information under section 1681i
(a)(5)(B) of this title.
(3) Significance of block. For purposes of this subsection, if a consumer reporting agency rescinds a block, the presence of
information in the file of a consumer prior to the blocking of such information is not evidence of whether the consumer knew
or should have known that the consumer obtained possession of any goods, services, or money as a result of the block.
(d) Exception for resellers.
(1) No reseller file. This section shall not apply to a consumer reporting agency, if the consumer reporting agency—
(A) is a reseller;
(B) is not, at the time of the request of the consumer under subsection (a) of this section, otherwise furnishing or reselling
a consumer report concerning the information identified by the consumer; and
(C) informs the consumer, by any means, that the consumer may report the identity theft to the Bureau to obtain
consumer information regarding identity theft.
(2) Reseller with file. The sole obligation of the consumer reporting agency under this section, with regard to any request of a
consumer under this section, shall be to block the consumer report maintained by the consumer reporting agency from any
subsequent use, if—
(A) the consumer, in accordance with the provisions of subsection (a) of this section, identifies, to a consumer reporting
agency, information in the file of the consumer that resulted from identity theft; and 
(B) the consumer reporting agency is a reseller of the identified information.
(3) Notice. In carrying out its obligation under paragraph (2), the reseller shall promptly provide a notice to the consumer of
the decision to block the file. Such notice shall contain the name, address, and telephone number of each consumer reporting
agency from which the consumer information was obtained for resale.
(e) Exception for verification companies. The provisions of this section do not apply to a check services company, acting as such,
which issues authorizations for the purpose of approving or processing negotiable instruments, electronic fund transfers, or similar
methods of payments, except that, beginning 4 business days after receipt of information described in paragraphs (1) through (3) of
subsection (a) of this section, a check services company shall not report to a national consumer reporting agency described in section
1681a (p) of this title, any information identified in the subject identity theft report as resulting from identity theft.
(f) Access to blocked information by law enforcement agencies. No provision of this section shall be construed as requiring a
consumer reporting agency to prevent a Federal, State, or local law enforcement agency from accessing blocked information in a
consumer file to which the agency could otherwise obtain access under this subchapter.

> Content Snippet:
> [L1] ﻿Alan Nguyen
> [L2] 11150 Rhode Island Ave S
> [L3] Bloomington, MN 55438
> [L4] SSN: XXX-XX-5713
> [L5] DOB: 07/25/1995
> [L6] TransUnion LLC
> [L7] LEGAL & Office of the General Counsel
> [L8] 555 West Adams Street
> [L9] Chicago, IL 60661
> [L10] Date: January 23rd 2026
> [L11] Re: Final Notice of Willful Non-Compliance, Demand for Cure, and Intent to File Suit - FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)
> [L12] To Whom It May Concern,
> [L13] This letter constitutes formal notice of willful and continuing non-compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”) following TransUnion’s repeated failure to comply with mandatory statutory duties, failure to respond to certified-mail notices with proof of delivery, and reliance on unlawful internal practices after actual notice.
> [L14] This notice is sent in good faith to provide one final opportunity to cure.
> [L15] ________________
> [L16] 
> [L17] 
> [L18] I. UNDISPUTED FACTS
> [L19] 1. TransUnion received multiple complete FCRA §605B identity theft submissions, each containing:
> [L20]    * A valid FTC Identity Theft Report
> [L21]    * Proof of identity
> [L22]    * Proof of address
> [L23]    * Written identification of alleged fraudulent hard inquiries
> [L24]    * A sworn statement that the transactions were not authorized
> [L25] 2. Receipt of these submissions is documented by certified-mail return receipts and CFPB complaint records.
> [L26] 3. Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion was required to:
> [L27]    * Block the identified information within four (4) business days, or
> [L28]    * Promptly issue a written denial citing §605B(c) and explaining with specificity the statutory basis for refusal.
> [L29] 4. TransUnion did neither.
> [L30] Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 907 (7th Cir. 2007).
> [L31] ________________
> [L32] 
> [L33] 
> [L34] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES
> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

> [L1] §1681i(a)(6)(B)(iii) (FCRA §611). 
> [L2] Willful violations trigger statutory and punitive damages under §1681n. Negligent violations are 
> [L3] actionable under §1681o. 
> [L4] Timeline of §605B Submissions (Fully Documented) 
> [L5] Since June 5, 2025, I submitted multiple complete §605B identity theft block requests, each 
> [L6] via trackable certified mail with full documentation + signature of receipt, including: 
> [L7] ● FTC Report 
> [L8] ● Notarized Affidavit 
> [L9] ● Government ID 
> [L10] ● Proof of Address 
> [L11] Submission Dates: 
> [L12] ● June 9, 2025 (CFPB Complaint 250609-21400333)
> [L13] ● June 13, 2025 
> [L14] ● June 16, 2025 (CFPB Complaint #250616-21593904) 
> [L15] ● July 4th, 2025 (post CFPB Complaint #250704-22063859) 
> [L16] Despite meeting every statutory requirement, TransUnion refused to block fraudulent data 
> [L17] within 4 business days as required by §605B(a). 
> [L18] Denial Reasons Provided by TransUnion 
> [L19] (Calls have been recorded, documented, and transcribed via Minnesota 1 way consent laws. 
> [L20] Although as a courtesy, all supervisors were informed beforehand of the recording & 
> [L21] documentation of the calls) 
> [L22] In calls and responses, TransUnion representatives provided unlawful reasons for refusing my 
> [L23] §605B requests: 
> [L24] 1. Creditor deletion letters required: 
> [L25] 12195064.1.3-10 <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 4 / 10> ○ Repeatedly demanded letters from creditors as the “only” way, even though 
> [L26] FCRA §605B has no such requirement. 
> [L27] 2. “System will not allow” removals: 
> [L28] ○ Special Handling Supervisor(s), alleged the system prevented deletion even with 
> [L29] valid documentation. 
> [L30] 3. Internal policy overrides law: 
> [L31] ○ Employees cited “internal policy” to ignore §605B’s 4-day block requirement. 
> [L32] 4. Rejecting valid FTC Reports and affidavits: 
> [L33] ○ No deficiencies in my documentation were ever identified.
> [L34] ○ Rejecting Valid FTC Reports and Affidavits Without Lawful Justification 
> [L35] Despite my submission of a valid FTC Identity Theft Report, sworn 
> [L36] affidavit, and all required supporting documents under FCRA §605B, 
> [L37] TransUnion has repeatedly rejected my request to block fraudulent 
> [L38] inquiries without identifying any specific deficiency in the materials 
> [L39] provided - either in writing or during recorded phone calls with supervisors 
> [L40] from their Fraud Department. 
> [L41] This violates multiple provisions of federal law: 
> [L42] 1. FCRA §605B(b)(2): 
> [L43] "An identity theft report may be a report to a law enforcement 
> [L44] agency or the Federal Trade Commission." 
> [L45] This statute explicitly confirms that a FTC Identity Theft Report 
> [L46] (Affidavit) is legally valid for identity theft blocking requests. It does not 
> [L47] require a police report, nor may the CRA reject an FTC report based 
> [L48] solely on form preference. 
> [L49] 2. FCRA §605B(c)(2): 
> [L50] "The consumer reporting agency may not refuse to block the 
> [L51] information on the grounds that the consumer has not provided any 
> [L52] additional documentation or information, other than as described in 
> [L53] subsection (b)." 
> [L54] Once the FTC Report, affidavit, ID, and proof of address are submitted 
> [L55] - which I provided in full - TransUnion is legally prohibited from requiring 
> [L56] any additional documents or imposing further barriers. 
> [L57] 12195064.1.4-10 <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 10> 3. FCRA §611(a)(6)(B)(iii): Requirement to Identify

> [L25] ________________
> [L26] 
> [L27] 
> [L28] III. STATUTORY FRAMEWORK — §605B (BLACK-LETTER LAW)
> [L29] 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a) provides:
> [L30] A consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from identity theft not later than 4 business days after receipt of:
> [L31]                         1. appropriate proof of identity
> [L32] 
> [L33]                         2. a copy of an identity theft report
> [L34] 
> [L35]                         3. identification of the information to be blocked
> [L36] 
> [L37]                         4. a statement that the information is not related to any transaction by the consumer
> [L38] 
> [L39] The statute is mandatory, not discretionary.
> [L40] The only basis to refuse a block appears in §605B(c) and requires a specific determination, communicated to the consumer, that:
> [L41]                            * the identity theft report was materially false, or
> [L42] 
> [L43]                            * the consumer misrepresented a material fact
> [L44] 
> [L45] ________________
> [L46] 
> [L47] 
> [L48] IV. PROOF OF CONSUMER COMPLIANCE
> [L49] TransUnion has already acknowledged receipt of:
> [L50]                               * proof of identity
> [L51] 
> [L52]                               * a valid identity theft report (FTC-compliant)
> [L53] 
> [L54]                               * sworn non-authorization statements
> [L55] 
> [L56]                               * clear identification of the inquiries at issue
> [L57] 
> [L58] At no point did TransUnion issue a written notice stating:
> [L59]                                  * which statutory element was allegedly missing
> [L60] 
> [L61]                                  * which material misrepresentation was claimed
> [L62] 
> [L63]                                  * or that §605B(c) was being invoked
> [L64] 
> [L65] ________________
> [L66] 
> [L67] 
> [L68] V. TRANSUNION’S ADMISSIONS AND CONDUCT
> [L69] On recorded calls, multiple TransUnion representatives & supervisors, including Hazel Smith, stated many times, in substance:
> [L70]         
> [L71]                                     * Acknowledged and affirmed that they received all 4 necessary requirements & documentation from the consumer as written in FCRA 605B
> [L72] 
> [L73] 
> [L74]                                     * “We received your documents.”
> [L75] 
> [L76]                                     * “We follow FCRA.”
> [L77] 
> [L78]                                     * “We cannot remove inquiries without creditor deletion letters.”
> [L79] 
> [L80]                                     * “We are not here to discuss the law.”
> [L81] 
> [L82]                                     * “You must have a freeze or fraud alert for us to treat this as identity theft.”
> [L83]

> [L87] 
> [L88]                                        * who placed or removed it
> [L89] 
> [L90]                                        * whether TransUnion can disclose its own records
> [L91] 
> [L92] These admissions are preserved.
> [L93] ________________
> [L94] 
> [L95] 
> [L96] VI. ANTICIPATED DEFENSES — AND WHY THEY FAIL
> [L97] A. “You Called and Unfroze the Account”
> [L98] Even if assumed true (which is disputed):
> [L99]                                           * §605B does not condition relief on maintaining a freeze
> [L100] 
> [L101]                                           * No statutory provision allows denial of a block based on post-submission account activity
> [L102] 
> [L103]                                           * TransUnion has not produced records, authentication logs, or written findings
> [L104] 
> [L105]                                           * No §605B(c) determination was issued
> [L106] 
> [L107] Belief is not evidence. Suspicion is not statutory authority.
> [L108] ________________
> [L109] 
> [L110] 
> [L111] B. “A Freeze or Fraud Alert Is Required”
> [L112] False.
> [L113]                                              * §605B does not list a freeze or fraud alert as a prerequisite
> [L114] 
> [L115]                                              * Congress knew how to require them and did not
> [L116] 
> [L117]                                              * TransUnion cannot add conditions not found in the statute
> [L118] 
> [L119] ________________
> [L120] 
> [L121] 
> [L122] C.

> [L1] ﻿Alan Nguyen
> [L2] 11150 Rhode Island Ave S
> [L3] Bloomington, MN 55438
> [L4] SSN: XXX-XX-5713
> [L5] DOB: 07/25/1995
> [L6] TransUnion LLC
> [L7] LEGAL & Office of the General Counsel
> [L8] 555 West Adams Street
> [L9] Chicago, IL 60661
> [L10] Date: January 23rd 2026
> [L11] Re: Final Notice of Willful Non-Compliance, Demand for Cure, and Intent to File Suit - FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2)
> [L12] To Whom It May Concern,
> [L13] This letter constitutes formal notice of willful and continuing non-compliance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act (“FCRA”) following TransUnion’s repeated failure to comply with mandatory statutory duties, failure to respond to certified-mail notices with proof of delivery, and reliance on unlawful internal practices after actual notice.
> [L14] This notice is sent in good faith to provide one final opportunity to cure.
> [L15] ________________
> [L16] 
> [L17] 
> [L18] I. UNDISPUTED FACTS
> [L19] 1. TransUnion received multiple complete FCRA §605B identity theft submissions, each containing:
> [L20]    * A valid FTC Identity Theft Report
> [L21]    * Proof of identity
> [L22]    * Proof of address
> [L23]    * Written identification of alleged fraudulent hard inquiries
> [L24]    * A sworn statement that the transactions were not authorized
> [L25] 2. Receipt of these submissions is documented by certified-mail return receipts and CFPB complaint records.
> [L26] 3. Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a), TransUnion was required to:
> [L27]    * Block the identified information within four (4) business days, or
> [L28]    * Promptly issue a written denial citing §605B(c) and explaining with specificity the statutory basis for refusal.
> [L29] 4. TransUnion did neither.
> [L30] Courts have recognized that the §605B identity theft block is a mandatory, non-discretionary duty once a compliant submission is received, and that failure to timely block constitutes a standalone violation regardless of creditor response, including within the Seventh Circuit. See Gillespie v. Trans Union Corp., 482 F.3d 907 (7th Cir. 2007).
> [L31] ________________
> [L32] 
> [L33] 
> [L34] II. UNLAWFUL DENIAL PRACTICES
> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

> [L35] Instead of complying with federal law, TransUnion:
> [L36] * Asserted that my FTC Identity Theft Report and supporting documentation were “invalid”, without identifying any deficiency, omission, or statutory basis;
> [L37] * Failed to explain how or why the documentation allegedly failed to satisfy §605B(a);
> [L38] * Locked my consumer account, denying access to my credit file in violation of §1681g;
> [L39] Courts have held that restricting or conditioning a consumer’s access to their own credit file violates §1681g and materially supports a finding of willful noncompliance. See Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010).
> [L40] * Conditioned §605B compliance on:
> [L41]    * Waiting for creditor responses,
> [L42]    * Obtaining creditor confirmation letters,
> [L43]    * Internal “company policy” or “system limitations.”
> [L44] None of these conditions exist in §605B or elsewhere in the FCRA.
> [L45] They are legally void.
> [L46] Federal courts have consistently held that a consumer reporting agency acts willfully under the FCRA when it adopts internal interpretations or practices that contradict the plain text of the statute after receiving notice of noncompliance. See Safeco Ins. Co. of Am. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 (2007) (reckless disregard includes conduct presenting an unjustifiably high risk of violating the statute that is either known or so obvious it should be known); see also Cushman v. Trans Union Corp., 115 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 1997) (willfulness established where a CRA relied on procedures that ignored statutory obligations after notice).

> [L28] III. STATUTORY FRAMEWORK — §605B (BLACK-LETTER LAW)
> [L29] 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2(a) provides:
> [L30] A consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from identity theft not later than 4 business days after receipt of:
> [L31]                         1. appropriate proof of identity
> [L32] 
> [L33]                         2. a copy of an identity theft report
> [L34] 
> [L35]                         3. identification of the information to be blocked
> [L36] 
> [L37]                         4. a statement that the information is not related to any transaction by the consumer
> [L38] 
> [L39] The statute is mandatory, not discretionary.
> [L40] The only basis to refuse a block appears in §605B(c) and requires a specific determination, communicated to the consumer, that:
> [L41]                            * the identity theft report was materially false, or
> [L42] 
> [L43]                            * the consumer misrepresented a material fact
> [L44] 
> [L45] ________________
> [L46] 
> [L47] 
> [L48] IV. PROOF OF CONSUMER COMPLIANCE
> [L49] TransUnion has already acknowledged receipt of:
> [L50]                               * proof of identity
> [L51] 
> [L52]                               * a valid identity theft report (FTC-compliant)
> [L53] 
> [L54]                               * sworn non-authorization statements
> [L55] 
> [L56]                               * clear identification of the inquiries at issue
> [L57] 
> [L58] At no point did TransUnion issue a written notice stating:
> [L59]                                  * which statutory element was allegedly missing
> [L60] 
> [L61]                                  * which material misrepresentation was claimed
> [L62] 
> [L63]                                  * or that §605B(c) was being invoked
> [L64] 
> [L65] ________________
> [L66] 
> [L67] 
> [L68] V. TRANSUNION’S ADMISSIONS AND CONDUCT
> [L69] On recorded calls, multiple TransUnion representatives & supervisors, including Hazel Smith, stated many times, in substance:
> [L70]         
> [L71]                                     * Acknowledged and affirmed that they received all 4 necessary requirements & documentation from the consumer as written in FCRA 605B
> [L72] 
> [L73] 
> [L74]                                     * “We received your documents.”
> [L75] 
> [L76]                                     * “We follow FCRA.”
> [L77] 
> [L78]                                     * “We cannot remove inquiries without creditor deletion letters.”
> [L79] 
> [L80]                                     * “We are not here to discuss the law.”
> [L81] 
> [L82]                                     * “You must have a freeze or fraud alert for us to treat this as identity theft.”
> [L83] 
> [L84]                                     * Conflicting statements regarding whether:
> [L85] 
> [L86]                                        * a freeze ever existed
> [L87] 
> [L88]                                        * who placed or removed it
> [L89] 
> [L90]                                        * whether TransUnion can disclose its own records
> [L91] 
> [L92] These admissions are preserved.
> [L93] ________________
> [L94] 
> [L95] 
> [L96] VI. ANTICIPATED DEFENSES — AND WHY THEY FAIL
> [L97] A. “You Called and Unfroze the Account”
> [L98] Even if assumed true (which is disputed):
> [L99]                                           * §605B does not condition relief on maintaining a freeze
> [L100] 
> [L101]                                           * No statutory provision allows denial of a block based on post-submission account activity
> [L102] 
> [L103]                                           * TransUnion has not produced records, authentication logs, or written findings
> [L104] 
> [L105]                                           * No §605B(c) determination was issued
> [L106] 
> [L107] Belief is not evidence. Suspicion is not statutory authority.
> [L108] ________________
> [L109] 
> [L110] 
> [L111] B. “A Freeze or Fraud Alert Is Required”
> [L112] False.
> [L113]                                              * §605B does not list a freeze or fraud alert as a prerequisite
> [L114] 
> [L115]                                              * Congress knew how to require them and did not
> [L116] 
> [L117]                                              * TransUnion cannot add conditions not found in the statute
> [L118] 
> [L119] ________________

TransUnion has suggested that it “believes” I contacted TransUnion to remove a freeze and therefore attributes the identity-theft–related inquiries to me.

> I. STATUTORY FOUNDATION (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
> FCRA §605B (15 U.S.C. §1681c-2) requires a consumer reporting agency (“CRA”) to block the reporting of any information identified by the consumer as resulting from alleged identity theft no later than four (4) business days after receipt of:
> 	1	Appropriate proof of identity of the consumer;
> 	2	A copy of an identity-theft report (an FTC Identity Theft Report qualifies); and
> 	3	Identification of the information and a statement that it is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer.
> 
> 
> Sole statutory exception (§605B(c)): A CRA may decline or rescind a block only if it determines the block was in error or facts were misrepresented, and must promptly notify the consumer in writing with the reasons.
> 
> The statute does not authorize creditor deletion letters, credit freezes, fraud alerts, or other extra-statutory prerequisites.
> 
> 
> 
> I-A. STATUTORY LIMITERS (WHAT §605B(c) AND §605B(d) DO - AND DO NOT DO)
> 	•	§605B(c) - Decline/Rescind Authority (narrow): TransUnion may decline or rescind only if it reasonably determines one of (A) error, (B) material misrepresentation, or (C) consumer obtained goods/services/money from the blocked transaction - and must then provide prompt written notice.
> 	•	§605B(d) - Reseller Exception (limited): Applies only to a CRA if it is acting as a reseller under the statute’s definition and meets the specific conditions in §605B(d).
> 	•	TransUnion has not provided any written position invoking §605B(d) or identifying itself as a reseller-only file for the disputed information, nor has it issued the notices §605B(d) describes. Therefore, TransUnion’s denials have been operationally based on extra-statutory “policy/system” conditions, not a documented statutory exception.

> [L5] I-A. STATUTORY LIMITERS (WHAT §605B(c) AND §605B(d) DO - AND DO NOT DO)
> [L6] 	•	§605B(c) - Decline/Rescind Authority (narrow): TransUnion may decline or rescind only if it reasonably determines one of (A) error, (B) material misrepresentation, or (C) consumer obtained goods/services/money from the blocked transaction - and must then provide prompt written notice.
> [L7] 	•	§605B(d) - Reseller Exception (limited): Applies only to a CRA if it is acting as a reseller under the statute’s definition and meets the specific conditions in §605B(d).
> [L8] 	•	TransUnion has not provided any written position invoking §605B(d) or identifying itself as a reseller-only file for the disputed information, nor has it issued the notices §605B(d) describes. Therefore, TransUnion’s denials have been operationally based on extra-statutory “policy/system” conditions, not a documented statutory exception.
> [L9] 	•	TransUnion has repeatedly refused to provide reasoning behind 605B declinations & compliance, stating things like “police report is required” refusing to accept the FTC report + Affidavit in lieu as the law states, as well as stating that the “FTC report is invalid” and refusing to provide any reasoning for why, and how to cure besides telling the consumer to send in another report, even after validating all 4 requirements from 605B in writing, continuing to decline further details.

> [L5] I-A. STATUTORY LIMITERS (WHAT §605B(c) AND §605B(d) DO - AND DO NOT DO)
> [L6] 	•	§605B(c) - Decline/Rescind Authority (narrow): TransUnion may decline or rescind only if it reasonably determines one of (A) error, (B) material misrepresentation, or (C) consumer obtained goods/services/money from the blocked transaction - and must then provide prompt written notice.
> [L7] 	•	§605B(d) - Reseller Exception (limited): Applies only to a CRA if it is acting as a reseller under the statute’s definition and meets the specific conditions in §605B(d).
> [L8] 	•	TransUnion has not provided any written position invoking §605B(d) or identifying itself as a reseller-only file for the disputed information, nor has it issued the notices §605B(d) describes. Therefore, TransUnion’s denials have been operationally based on extra-statutory “policy/system” conditions, not a documented statutory exception.

> [L14] SECTION 2 — WHAT THE LAW REQUIRES (IN SIMPLE TERMS)
> [L15] 2.1 Identity Theft Blocking Under Federal Law (FCRA §605B)
> [L16] Under 15 U.S.C. §1681c-2, when a consumer submits:
> [L17] * An FTC Identity Theft Report (or police report)
> [L18] * Proof of identity
> [L19] * Proof of address
> [L20] * A written statement identifying the fraudulent items
> [L21] The consumer reporting agency MUST block the fraudulent information within four (4) business days.
> [L22] There is:
> [L23] * No discretion
> [L24] * No investigation requirement
> [L25] * No creditor permission requirement
> [L26] * No police report requirement when an FTC report is provided
> [L27] This duty is mandatory, not optional.
> [L28] ________________

> [L31] Even if assumed true (which is disputed):

> [L45] False.
> [L46]                                              * §605B does not list a freeze or fraud alert as a prerequisite

> [L1] The statute does not authorize creditor deletion letters, credit freezes, fraud alerts, or other extra-statutory prerequisites.
> [L2] 
> [L3] 
> [L4] 
> [L5] I-A. STATUTORY LIMITERS (WHAT §605B(c) AND §605B(d) DO - AND DO NOT DO)
> [L6] 	•	§605B(c) - Decline/Rescind Authority (narrow): TransUnion may decline or rescind only if it reasonably determines one of (A) error, (B) material misrepresentation, or (C) consumer obtained goods/services/money from the blocked transaction - and must then provide prompt written notice.
> [L7] 	•	§605B(d) - Reseller Exception (limited): Applies only to a CRA if it is acting as a reseller under the statute’s definition and meets the specific conditions in §605B(d).
> [L8] 	•	TransUnion has not provided any written position invoking §605B(d) or identifying itself as a reseller-only file for the disputed information, nor has it issued the notices §605B(d) describes. Therefore, TransUnion’s denials have been operationally based on extra-statutory “policy/system” conditions, not a documented statutory exception.
> [L9] 	•	TransUnion has repeatedly refused to provide reasoning behind 605B declinations & compliance, stating things like “police report is required” refusing to accept the FTC report + Affidavit in lieu as the law states, as well as stating that the “FTC report is invalid” and refusing to provide any reasoning for why, and how to cure besides telling the consumer to send in another report, even after validating all 4 requirements from 605B in writing, continuing to decline further details.
> [L10] That stays strictly within what you can prove: no written statutory exception notice.
> [L11] 
> [L12] 
> [L13] 
> [L14] II. COMPLETENESS & ADMISSIONS
> [L15] TransUnion representatives confirmed receipt of all §605B items, including:

> [L17] 	•	An FTC Identity Theft Report executed under penalty of perjury;
> [L18] 	•	Identification of the identity-theft-related hard inquiries and a statement of non-authorization.
> [L19] 	•	All four statutory prerequisites under §605B were satisfied and acknowledged by TransUnion.
> 
> 
> [L20] Despite receipt, TransUnion did not block the information within four business days and never issued a §605B(c) written determination.

> [L23]
